units.translation: Pollux 2, 125 attributes it to Aeschylus by mistake, since it is from Aristophanes' Frogs 823.

ἀπερωπός [inhuman, savage] Kusterus on Hesychius s.v., ἀπέρωτος [unloved] M, with the letter τ made from π, which those who collated the codex before me overlooked. The scholiast reads ἀπερωπός [inhuman, savage], who explains it as ἀντὶ τοῦ στυγνός [instead of 'hateful'], and with similar adjectives Etym. M. p. 120, 41 also interprets it, and no doubt from this verse of Aeschylus Phrynichus in Bekker's Anecdota p. 8, 8. ἀπέρωπος [unloved] (with this accent): σημαίνει ἀναιδής, σκληρός, τραχύς, οἷον ἀπερίοπτος καὶ ἀπερίβλεπτος, ὃν οὐκ ἄν τις περιωπήσαιτο διὰ τὴν ἀηδίαν. καὶ ἀπέρωπον οἷον τραχὺ καὶ ἀνατεταμένον [it means shameless, hard, rough, like 'not to be looked at' and 'not to be glanced at', whom no one would look upon because of the unpleasantness. And 'unloved' like rough and stretched out]. See L. Dindorf in Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 1293.

before an abominable man touches this skin

an abominable marriage, hateful to the house

to keep their hands off the immortals

the one who came into hatred with all the gods

which Thomas Magister explains as μὴ τοῖς φίλοις πεισθέντες [not obeying friends]
You tell incredible things, strangers, for me to hear,
